newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesia consultant upbeat on property market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesia consultant upbeat on property market.

text.p: One of Indonesia's major property consultants gave an upbeat view of the market in a quarterly review on Wednesday, but said the hotel sector faced an oversupply of rooms.
PT Procon Indah/Jones Lang Wootton said in its April-June review the strength of the Indonesian economy was expected to maintain demand growth in Jakarta.

"We've got record levels of demand really in all sectors -- retail, office and the apartment/condominium market -- and that's riding on the back of strong fundamental economic growth in Indonesia," said senior technical adviser Phil Simpson, director of JLW Asia.

"Overlaid against that, we've got record levels of supply, which are probably by most standards looking somewhat frightening, but they are being underpinned by that strong growth," Simpson told Reuters.

He said there should be a reasonable match between supply and demand in all sectors, with the exception of hotels where room supply was forecast to shoot up 136 percent over the next three years outstripping demand.
"But even there I think the demand fundamentals are sufficiently strong that by the time we get to the other side of the year 2000, we will see that correcting itself," he added.
The report said that overage office occupancies in the Jakarta central business district market increased by one percent during the quarter to 88.8 percent.

"Average rents increased by five percent during the review period and are expected to further increase until mid-1998 due to the limited supply of completed space," it said. But it warned developers they should be cautious over proposed construction in 1999, which could bring down average market occupancy to 83 percent.
The report also said there was growing concern over the pending oversupply of hotel rooms, although there was a growing niche market for moderately-priced rooms.

But it said that a major increase in the number of potential property projects unable to secure financing and "increasing prudence on the part of bankers" meant a widespread property market crash on the scale of Thailand was unlikely.
The central bank, Bank Indonesia, last week curbed loans for the purchase and development of property to prevent excessive bank lending to the sector.

Bayu Utomo, the consultancy's head of research, said he expected the cantral bank's move to have a stabilising effect on the market, hitting mainly medium and small developers with limited access to funds.
The big developers, he said, could still have recourse to other financial schemes, such as tapping the capital market, getting offshore loans and attracting foreign equity investors.
He also noted that many small developers were involved in low cost housing, which was specifically exempted from the loan ban.
Simpson said that despite the political uncertainty in the first part of the year leading up to the May 29 general elections, Indonesia was attracting a lot of foreign investment capital.

"It's fair to say that the last six months have seen more capital window shopping in Indonesia than we've ever seen before. They're very ready to buy and we're seeing the front end of some very substantial deals...," he said.

"We are seeing that these people are taking a view on Indonesia as being one of the few opportunity markets over the next two to three years," he added. "People are comfortable with where we are going in the long haul."
